course.note: Italian taught from Spanish, explained in Spanglish. Grammar order follows the MTC Italian Language Guide (2015), used as a blueprint only; all text is original. Draft: needs a fluent check.

lessons.title: How this course works
lessons.decision: Spanish is your shortcut, not your crutch

blocks.title: Why from Spanish
blocks.text: You already own like 80% of Italian, you just don't know it yet. Same Latin family, same gender system, same me gusta logic, a lot of the same verbs. So this course doesn't start from zero. It starts from your Spanish and only teaches what's different.

The explanations are in Spanglish on purpose. Si una idea sale mejor en español, it's in español. The point is speed, not purity.

The cues you translate are mixed too: sometimes English, sometimes Spanish, sometimes both. Tú dilo en italiano.
Every lesson teaches one decision. You say every answer out loud before you reveal it, then grade yourself honestly. Getting it wrong is how it works: a wrong guess sticks better than being told.

The biggest danger for a Spanish speaker isn't Italian being hard. It's Italian being too easy, so Spanish leaks in: es instead of è, muy instead of molto, pero instead of ma. Each lesson names the leak before you hit it.

Some sentences have a real recording by a native speaker from Tatoeba, credited under the speaker button. Everything else uses your device's Italian voice, which is fine for checking a word, not for training your ear. For the ear, use the Immersion card.

The robot button copies a practice prompt for any AI chat. AIs make mistakes, so if one disagrees with a lesson, trust the lesson.

lessons.title: Spanish eyes, Italian mouth
lessons.decision: c and g go soft before e and i

blocks.title: Why sound comes first
blocks.text: Italian spelling is as honest as Spanish, but a few letters are wired differently. If you read Italian with Spanish rules, people understand you, but you sound like a tourist from Madrid. Fix six things now and you never have to unlearn them.

C before e or i is English ch, not Spanish s/z. cena is CHEH-nah. ciao is CHOW: the i is only there to make the c soft, you don't say it.

G before e/i is English j: gelato is jeh-LAH-toh. Never the Spanish jota.

blocks.a: c + e = ch. La cena, same word as Spanish, Italian mouth.
g + e = English j. Same word as Spanish gente, totally different sound.

blocks.text:
So how do you get a hard k sound before e/i? Italian adds an h: che is KEH, chi is KEE. Backwards from Spanish, where ch is the soft one. Same with ghe/ghi: hard g.

Ojo: chi means who. che means que.

blocks.a: ch = k in Italian. Chiesa means iglesia.

blocks.text: gn is your ñ: bagno = BAH-ñoh. gli is like a ll said with the tongue flat, close to the lli in million: famiglia = fah-MEE-lyah. sc before e/i is English sh: scienza = SHEN-tsah. z is ts or dz, never Spanish s or th.

blocks.a: gli is one sound, a soft ly. The g is silent.

blocks.text: Last one, and it's the one Spanish speakers skip: double consonants are held longer. pala (shovel) vs palla (ball). nono (ninth) vs nonno (grandpa). You literally pause on the double letter. Si no lo haces, you're saying a different word.

blocks.a: Hold the nn, like the n in 'unknown'. Nono is ninth, nonno is grandpa.

blocks.text: Good news: stress works almost like Spanish. Most words hit the second-to-last syllable, and a written accent at the end (città, perché) means hit the last one. Italian just doesn't write accents in the middle of words, so telefono is te-LEH-fo-no and you learn it by ear.

unlocks: Pronunciation: c/g soft before e,i (ch, j) · ch/gh hard · gn = ñ · gli · sc = sh · z = ts · double consonants held
lessons.ai: Give me Italian words to read aloud that test c/g before e and i, ch/gh, gn, gli, sc, and double consonants. Ask me to describe how I'd say each, then correct me.

lessons.title: Fare conoscenza

blocks.title: Why this first
blocks.text: Before any grammar you need the ten seconds that open every conversation: hi, what's your name, where are you from, nice to meet you. Italians do this fast and warm. Get it smooth and people relax and slow down for you.

Ciao is hi and bye, for friends. With strangers or older people: buongiorno (until mid-afternoon) and buonasera (after). Salve is the safe neutral hello when you're not sure.

Name: mi chiamo Ethan. Literally me llamo, but the pronoun is mi, not me. Leak alert.

Asking: come ti chiami? (tú). Come is cómo, and the ti is your te. Formal: come si chiama?

Nice to meet you: piacere. Literally placer. Remember this word, it comes back big in lesson 11.

Where from: di dove sei? = ¿de dónde eres? Italian says di where Spanish says de, and dove is dónde.

Answer: sono di Salt Lake City or sono americano. Sono = soy. More on that next lesson.

Two more you'll use all day: grazie (GRAH-tsyeh, gracias) and prego (de nada, and also go ahead, please, after you). Per favore is por favor.

Leak alert: it's per, never por.

unlocks: mi chiamo / come ti chiami? / come si chiama?
lessons.ai: Role-play meeting me for the first time. Switch between a friend my age (tu) and an older stranger (formal), and correct my greetings.

lessons.title: Words you already own

blocks.title: Why this matters
blocks.text: Spanish already handed you thousands of Italian words. A few swaps unlock them all, so you can say real sentences next lesson instead of parroting phrases.
-ción → -zione, and it stays feminine: la nación → la nazione, la información → l'informazione. Plural is -zioni.
-dad → -tà, stressed on the end: la ciudad → la città, la universidad → l'università, la libertad → la libertà. These never change in the plural: le città.
-ble → -bile: posible → possibile, increíble → incredibile. And notice Italian loves doubling: posible has one s, possibile has two. -mente stays exactly the same: esattamente, finalmente.
Articles: il = el, la = la. Before a vowel both shrink to l'. Before s + consonant or z, el becomes lo: lo studente. Plurals: i / gli (masc), le (fem). Don't stress, you'll absorb these.
And one big leak: Spanish plurals add -s. Italian plurals change the last vowel: -o → -i, -a → -e. los libros → i libri, las casas → le case. No -s, ever.

lessons.ai: Give me Spanish nouns ending in -ción, -dad and -ble and have me convert them to Italian with the right article, singular and plural.

lessons.title: Essere
lessons.decision: one verb for ser and (mostly) estar

blocks.title: Why essere matters
blocks.text: Here's the gift: Italian mostly doesn't have your ser/estar split. Essere covers what Spanish splits in two, including location. Italians do have stare, but it only does a few jobs (lesson 26). So the leak to watch is reaching for stare every time you'd say estar.

sono: soy / estoy
sei: eres / estás
è: es / está
siamo: somos / estamos
siete: sois / estáis
sono: son / están

Yes, sono is both I am and they are. Context sorts it out.
The accent on è matters. e without it means y (and). È means es/está. Spanish leak alert: never say es.
See that? dov'è = dove + è squished. Location with essere, no estar needed. ¿Dónde estás? → dove sei?
Negation is no → non, in front of the verb: non sono stanco. And molto = muy/mucho. Leak: never muy.

unlocks: essere present: sono, sei, è, siamo, siete, sono — covers ser AND estar incl. location
lessons.ai: Give me sentences mixing ser and estar meanings in English or Spanish, and have me use essere for all of them. Flag if I use 'stare' or Spanish 'es'.

lessons.title: Avere
lessons.decision: avere = tener, and the h is silent

blocks.title: Why avere matters
blocks.text: Avere is your tener, and later it's also your haber: it builds the past tense in lesson 21. Learn it rock solid now and the whole past tense is half done.

ho: tengo
hai: tienes
ha: tiene
abbiamo: tenemos
avete: tenéis
hanno: tienen

The h is completely silent, it's only there to tell ho (I have) from o (or), and ha from a (to). So ho sounds like 'oh', hanno like ANN-noh.
Leak alert: pregunta is domanda. Spanish speakers want to say pregunta and it's not a word. And domandare means to ask, not to sue.

Same expressions as Spanish, mostly: ho fame (tengo hambre), ho sete (sed), ho freddo (frío), ho sonno (sueño), ho 20 anni (tengo 20 años). Ojo: anni with double n. Ani is... a body part. Hold that n.

blocks.en: how old are you? (cuántos años tienes)

blocks.text: One difference: tener que is not avere che. Obligation is its own verb, dovere, in lesson 8. Don't build ho che, it's not Italian.

unlocks: avere present: ho, hai, ha, abbiamo, avete, hanno (h silent)
avere expressions: fame, sete, freddo, sonno, X anni
lessons.ai: Ask me questions about what I have, how old people are, and if I'm hungry/cold/sleepy. Make me answer with avere. Catch me if I say 'pregunta' or 'ho che'.

lessons.title: Questo e quello
lessons.decision: questo = este, quello = ese AND aquel

blocks.title: Why this
blocks.text: Pointing at stuff is half of real conversation. Spanish has three distances (este, ese, aquel). Italian has two. Less to learn, one thing to unlearn.

questo / questa / questi / queste: este, esta, estos, estas. It works like any -o adjective.

quello: ese AND aquel. Spanish ese doesn't have its own word, it folds into quello.

The tricky part: quello in front of a noun changes shape like the article il/lo/l'/i/gli. Think 'que' + the article:
quel libro (il libro)
quello studente (lo studente)
quell'amico (l'amico)
quei libri (i libri)
quegli amici (gli amici)
quella / quelle for feminine.

unlocks: quello = ese/aquel; before nouns: quel, quello, quell', quei, quegli, quella, quelle (follows il/lo/l'/i/gli)
lessons.ai: Point at imaginary things near and far and have me say 'this X' and 'that X' in Italian, singular and plural, with the right quello form.

lessons.title: Questo, quello, standing alone

blocks.title: Why this
blocks.text: When the noun is obvious you drop it: quiero ese, esto es mío. Italian does the same, and it's actually simpler than the last lesson.
Alone, without a noun, they're always the full form: questo, questa, questi, queste, quello, quella, quelli, quelle. No quel / quegli games. That's only before a noun.
Spanish has a neuter esto / eso for 'this thing, that idea'. Italian just uses questo and quello (masculine) for that.
Che cos'è? is the standard 'what is it?'. Che = qué, cosa = cosa. You can also just say cos'è?
Small preview: voglio = quiero. Full story next lesson.

unlocks: Demonstrative pronouns: questo/a/i/e, quello/a/i/e (full forms when alone)
lessons.ai: Hold up imaginary objects and ask me 'che cos'è?'. Make me answer and point using questo/quello alone, no noun.

lessons.title: Volere e dovere

blocks.title: Why this
blocks.text: This is where you start talking for real. One conjugated verb + any infinitive = a sentence. Exactly like quiero comer, debo ir. Every infinitive you know just became usable.
Infinitives: -ar → -are, -er → -ere, -ir → -ire. hablar → parlare, comer → mangiare (ok, that one's different), vivir → vivere, dormir → dormire. Most Spanish verbs just grow an -e.

volere (querer): voglio, vuoi, vuole, vogliamo, volete, vogliono.
dovere (deber / tener que): devo, devi, deve, dobbiamo, dovete, devono.
Dovere covers both deber and tener que. One word, less thinking. lavorare = trabajar (think 'labor').
Polite tip: voglio sounds pushy when ordering at a bar. Italians say vorrei (quisiera). You'll build it in lesson 29, but you can steal it now: vorrei un caffè.

unlocks: volere + inf (voglio, vuoi, vuole, vogliamo, volete, vogliono)
dovere + inf = deber/tener que (devo, devi, deve, dobbiamo, dovete, devono)
lessons.ai: Give me sentences with want to / have to + verb, in English or Spanish, and make me use volere or dovere + infinitive. Mix persons.

lessons.title: Sapere

blocks.title: Why this
blocks.text: Sapere is saber, and it works the same: knowing facts and knowing how to do stuff. Sé nadar → so nuotare.

so, sai, sa, sappiamo, sapete, sanno.

Leak alert: I know is so, not sé. Short and weird, says it like 'soh'.
Italians almost always add lo: non lo so (I don't know it). Bare non so exists but non lo so is the reflex. Learn it as one chunk.
And conocer (people, places) is conoscere: conosco, conosci, conosce. Same split as Spanish. Conosco Roma, so che è bella.
Notice: no personal a. Italian doesn't put a before people as objects. Conozco a María → conosco Maria.

unlocks: sapere present: so, sai, sa, sappiamo, sapete, sanno; + infinitive = know how to
lessons.ai: Ask me what I and other people know how to do, and who/what we know. Make me choose sapere or conoscere and catch any personal 'a'.

lessons.title: Potere

blocks.title: Why this
blocks.text: Potere is poder. With volere, dovere, sapere and now potere, you have four openings and every infinitive behind them.

posso, puoi, può, possiamo, potete, possono.

Può has an accent: puede. Posso? alone means ¿puedo? / may I?, super useful when you walk into a shop or reach for a chair.
See aiutarmi? Pronoun glued on the end of the infinitive, like ayudarme. Italian drops the final -e first: aiutare + mi → aiutarmi.
Mix time. Pick the opening:

items.en: do you know how to cook?

unlocks: potere present: posso, puoi, può, possiamo, potete, possono
pronouns attach to infinitive minus -e: aiutarmi
lessons.ai: Mix volere, dovere, sapere and potere. Give me a situation and make me choose the right opening + infinitive.

lessons.title: Piacere
lessons.decision: mi piace works exactly like me gusta

blocks.title: Why this
blocks.text: Free lesson. Gustar logic transfers 100%: the thing does the pleasing, you're the indirect object. English speakers suffer here. You don't.

mi piace = me gusta
ti piace = te gusta
gli piace = le gusta (a él)
le piace = le gusta (a ella / usted)
ci piace = nos gusta
vi piace = os gusta
gli piace = les gusta

Plural thing: piacciono. Me gustan los gatos → mi piacciono i gatti.
Italian puts the article on countries: l'Italia, la Spagna, gli Stati Uniti.
Leak: gli (to him) vs le (to her). Spanish uses le for both. Italian splits by gender. A me piace = a mí me gusta, but Italian says it with just a me piace, no double pronoun.

blocks.en: a mí me gusta, a él no
blocks.es: a me piace, a lui no

lessons.ai: Ask me what I and others like and don't like. Include plural things so I need piacciono, and check gli vs le.

lessons.title: Fare
lessons.decision: faccio = hago, fa freddo = hace frío

blocks.title: Why this
blocks.text: Fare is hacer, and it's in a huge chunk of everyday phrases: weather, questions, going for a walk, taking a shower.
faccio, fai, fa, facciamo, fate, fanno.
Leak alert: caldo means hot, not soup broth. And freddo is cold. On faucets, C is caldo = hot. Seriously, don't burn yourself.
Fare-phrases worth stealing whole: fare una domanda (hacer una pregunta), fare colazione (desayunar), fare la doccia (bañarse), fare una passeggiata (dar un paseo).

blocks.en: I want to ask a question
what are you all doing tonight?

unlocks: fare present: faccio, fai, fa, facciamo, fate, fanno
fare + noun phrases: colazione, doccia, una domanda, una passeggiata
lessons.ai: Chat with me about my day and the weather using fare. Use fare-phrases and see if I can produce them.

lessons.title: Andare
lessons.decision: vado = voy, but not for the future

blocks.title: Why this
blocks.text: Andare is ir. And here's the most important leak in the whole course: Spanish uses voy a + infinitive for the future. Italian doesn't. Vado a mangiare only means you are physically going somewhere to eat.

vado, vai, va, andiamo, andate, vanno.

Andiamo! = ¡vamos!
Contractions: a + il = al, a + la = alla, a + i = ai. Like al in Spanish, but more of them. Also al mare is the beach-going phrase; la spiaggia is the sand itself.
Notice: no a before dove. Dove vai? straight.

So how do you say voy a comer (future)? For now: the plain present does it. Stasera mangio la pizza = I'm eating pizza tonight. Italians use the present for planned stuff all the time. Real future comes in lesson 27.

unlocks: andare present: vado, vai, va, andiamo, andate, vanno
a + article: al, allo, alla, all', ai, agli, alle
NO 'andare a + inf' future; use present
lessons.ai: Ask where I and others are going. Throw in 'voy a + verb' future sentences in Spanish and make sure I don't translate them with andare.

lessons.title: Venire

blocks.title: Why this
blocks.text: Venire = venir, and the forms are basically your Spanish with an Italian accent. Quick win.

vengo, vieni, viene, veniamo, venite, vengono.

Compare: vengo, vienes, viene… The Spanish -es just becomes -i.
Con me, con te: Italian doesn't glue them like conmigo, contigo.
da = from (origin, coming from). Vengo da + place. Di is for 'I'm from' with essere: sono di…. Both fine; venire takes da.

blocks.en: are you all coming to the party?

blocks.text: Bonus: vieni qui! = ven acá. Short, you'll hear it from every nonna.

unlocks: venire present: vengo, vieni, viene, veniamo, venite, vengono
lessons.ai: Ask me who's coming where and from where. Mix in andare so I have to choose.

lessons.title: Che ore sono?

blocks.title: Why this
blocks.text: Time and dates are pure vocabulary, and close to Spanish. The pattern is the same son las tres, just Italian words.
Numbers 1–10: uno, due, tre, quattro, cinque, sei, sette, otto, nove, dieci. Leak: sei is six, and also 'you are'. Cinque is CHEEN-kweh.
Time: che ore sono? (literally 'what hours are'). Sono le tre = son las tres. One o'clock: è l'una. Noon mezzogiorno, midnight mezzanotte. E mezza = y media, e un quarto = y cuarto.
Days, all lowercase like Spanish: lunedì, martedì, mercoledì, giovedì, venerdì, sabato, domenica. The -dì is día. Today oggi, tomorrow domani, yesterday ieri.
No el before a day for a single occasion: sabato = el sábado. Il sabato = los sábados (every Saturday).

unlocks: che ore sono? sono le…/è l'una, e mezza, e un quarto, alle…
days of the week; il lunedì = every Monday
lessons.ai: Ask me what time things happen in my week and make me answer with times and days.

lessons.title: Parlo, parli, parla

blocks.title: Why this
blocks.text: Up to now you've hidden behind openings. Now every verb gets its own forms. Good news: the -o for 'I' is identical to Spanish, and the rest are close cousins.

parlare: parlo, parli, parla, parliamo, parlate, parlano.

Compare hablo, hablas, habla. The big swap: Spanish tú ends in -s, Italian tu always ends in -i.

-ere: scrivo, scrivi, scrive, scriviamo, scrivete, scrivono.
-ire: dormo, dormi, dorme, dormiamo, dormite, dormono.

Noi is always -iamo, any verb. One ending to rule them all.
Twist: many -ire verbs add -isc-: capire (entender) → capisco, capisci, capisce, capiamo, capite, capiscono. Also finire, preferire. Just like Spanish conozco grows a c.
Non capisco is going to save your life for the first month. Pair it with più piano, per favore (more slowly, please).

lessons.ai: Talk with me about my daily routine with regular verbs, all persons. Watch for Spanish -s on tu forms.

lessons.title: Mi alzo
lessons.decision: reflexives like Spanish, but ci and vi

blocks.title: Why this
blocks.text: Reflexive verbs work the way you already think: me levanto → mi alzo. Only the little pronouns change shape.

mi (me), ti (te), si (se), ci (nos), vi (os), si (se).

Leak alert: nos is ci, and Spanish se is si.
Hey look: lesson 2 was a reflexive all along. Chiamarsi = llamarse.
Ci vediamo! is the standard 'see you'. Say it as you leave.
Infinitive: drop -e and glue si: alzarsi, chiamarsi, divertirsi. With an opening: devo alzarmi presto (tengo que levantarme temprano).

unlocks: Reflexive pronouns mi, ti, si, ci, vi, si
lessons.ai: Ask about my morning routine and weekend using reflexive verbs. Catch 'nos' and 'se' leaks.

lessons.title: Lo, la, li, le
lessons.decision: lo and la like Spanish, but li for los

blocks.title: Why this
blocks.text: Replacing the thing with 'it' so you don't repeat yourself. Same position as Spanish: before the conjugated verb, glued to an infinitive.

mi, ti, lo, la, ci, vi, li, le.

The one to drill: los → li. Le here is las (direct object!), not Spanish le.
Before ho/hai/ha/hanno, lo and la usually shrink: l'ho, l'hai. L'ho visto (lo he visto) shows up a lot in lesson 21.

blocks.en: I want to see it (el libro)

unlocks: Direct object pronouns mi, ti, lo, la, ci, vi, li, le — before verb or glued to infinitive
lessons.ai: Make me replace objects with pronouns: give me a sentence with a noun, and I answer with lo/la/li/le.

lessons.title: Me lo, glielo

blocks.title: Why this
blocks.text: Two pronouns at once, like te lo doy. Spanish turns le lo into se lo. Italian turns it into glielo, one word. Weird-looking, same idea.
Indirect pronoun first, i → e: me lo, te lo, ce lo, ve lo. Te lo doy → te lo do.
To him / her / them: glie- + lo/la/li/le/ne, all one word: glielo, gliela, glieli, gliele. Se lo doy → glielo do. Same for him, her, usted.

blocks.en: se la doy (la carta, a ella)

blocks.text: Glued to an infinitive like Spanish: devo dirglielo (tengo que decírselo).

unlocks: Combined pronouns: me lo, te lo, ce lo, ve lo; glielo/gliela/glieli/gliele = se lo
dare (do, dai, dà), dire (dico, dici, dice)
lessons.ai: Give me sentences with a thing and a person ('I give the book to Marco') and make me replace both with combined pronouns.

lessons.title: Ne e ci

blocks.title: Why this
blocks.text: Two tiny words Spanish doesn't have, and Italians say them nonstop. Without them, your Italian sounds like translated Spanish. With them, you sound like you live there.
ne = 'of it / of them / some'. Spanish just drops it. ¿Cuántos hermanos tienes? Tengo dos. Italian needs the ne: ne ho due.

blocks.es: vuoi del caffè? sì, ne voglio un po'

blocks.text: ci = 'there' (allí, ahí) for a place already mentioned. ¿Vas a Roma? Sí, voy. → sì, ci vado. Without ci it sounds chopped.

blocks.es: vai al cinema? sì, ci vado

blocks.text: And c'è / ci sono = hay. C'è un problema = hay un problema. Ci sono tre gatti = hay tres gatos. Singular and plural, unlike Spanish.

unlocks: ne for quantities/of it: ne ho due
lessons.ai: Ask me quantity and place questions where Italian needs ne or ci, and ask what there is in places so I use c'è / ci sono.

lessons.title: Ho parlato
lessons.decision: Italian says 'I have spoken' where Spanish says hablé

blocks.title: Why this
blocks.text: The everyday past in Italian is avere + participle, like he hablado. But Italians use it for everything, including yesterday: ieri ho mangiato la pizza, where you'd say ayer comí. Your Spanish brain will want a one-word past. Don't.
Participles: -are → -ato, -ere → -uto, -ire → -ito. parlato, venduto, dormito. Almost Spanish -ado/-ido.
Then avere from lesson 5: ho parlato, hai parlato, ha parlato, abbiamo parlato, avete parlato, hanno parlato.
Pronouns go in front of the whole thing, like Spanish: l'ho comprato (lo he comprado / lo compré).
Just one catch, and it's the next lesson: some verbs use essere instead of avere.

unlocks: Passato prossimo with avere: ho + -ato/-uto/-ito, used for completed past (Spanish preterite AND perfect)
lessons.ai: Ask me what I did yesterday and last week. Make me answer with passato prossimo + avere. Flag any attempt at a one-word past.

lessons.title: Sono andato

blocks.title: Why this
blocks.text: Spanish lost this, but old Spanish had it: some verbs build the past with to be. Sono andato = fui (literally 'I am gone'). Get it wrong and Italians still understand you, but it screams foreigner.

The test: does the verb move you from A to B, or change your state, and it can't take an object? Then essere. andare, venire, arrivare, partire, uscire, entrare, tornare, restare, nascere, morire, diventare. And all reflexives.
With essere, the participle agrees like an adjective: sono andato (man), sono andata (woman), siamo andati, sono andate.
Reflexives too: mi sono alzato (me levanté). And essere's own past is with essere: sono stato (estuve, fui). Yes, it borrows stare's participle.

blocks.en: have you ever been to Italy? (tú)

unlocks: Passato prossimo with essere: motion/change verbs + reflexives; participle agrees (andato/a/i/e)
lessons.ai: Ask me about trips and where people went and came back, including women and groups, so I need agreement. Mix avere and essere verbs.

lessons.title: Fatto, detto, visto

blocks.title: Why this
blocks.text: The most common verbs have irregular participles. Good news, they look like Spanish: hecho → fatto, dicho → detto.
Prendere is the Italian workhorse: take, grab, order (prendo un caffè), catch a bus. Use it where Spanish uses tomar.

unlocks: Irregular participles: fatto, detto, visto, preso, scritto, letto, messo, aperto, venuto, bevuto
lessons.ai: Ask what I did, saw, said, read, took this week so I need irregular participles.

lessons.title: Parlavo

blocks.title: Why this
blocks.text: The imperfect is nearly identical in use to Spanish: background, habits, 'used to', what was going on. Cuando era niño, jugaba → quando ero bambino, giocavo. And the split with passato prossimo is your preterite/imperfect split.
Drop -re, add -vo, -vi, -va, -vamo, -vate, -vano. parlavo, vendevo, dormivo. Spanish -aba → Italian -ava, Spanish -ía → Italian -eva / -iva.

blocks.en: cuando era niño, jugaba al fútbol
blocks.es: quando ero bambino, giocavo a calcio

blocks.text: Event vs scene, same as Spanish: dormivo quando hai chiamato = dormía cuando llamaste. Imperfect is the scene, passato prossimo the event.

blocks.en: I was eating when he arrived

blocks.text: Fare → facevo (from old facere), dire → dicevo, bere → bevevo. Long stems come back in the imperfect.

unlocks: imperfetto = scene/habit, passato prossimo = event (like Spanish)
lessons.ai: Ask me about my childhood and interrupted actions so I have to choose imperfetto vs passato prossimo.

lessons.title: Ero

blocks.title: Why this
blocks.text: Essere in the imperfect is irregular and super common: how things were, how old you were, where you were.

ero, eri, era, eravamo, eravate, erano.

Leak: yo era is ero, not era. In Italian era is only he/she/it.
Remember essere = ser + estar. So estaba is ero too. One word again.
C'era / c'erano = había. And the classic: c'era una volta… = había una vez.

unlocks: essere imperfetto: ero, eri, era, eravamo, eravate, erano
lessons.ai: Ask me to describe places and people from my past: what they were like, where I was.

lessons.title: Sto parlando
lessons.decision: stare only for -ing and how you're doing

blocks.title: Why this
blocks.text: Finally, stare. It's your estar but with a small job description: stare + gerund for right-now actions, and come stai? / sto bene for how you're doing. Everything else estar does, essere does.

sto, stai, sta, stiamo, state, stanno.
Gerund: -are → -ando, -ere/-ire → -endo. parlando, scrivendo, dormendo. Spanish -iendo just loses the i.
Facendo, from facere again. Also dicendo, bevendo.
But: estoy cansado = sono stanco. Está en casa = è a casa. If there's no -ndo and it's not 'how are you', it's essere.

unlocks: stare: sto, stai, sta, stiamo, state, stanno
stare + gerund (-ando/-endo) for actions in progress
stare for wellbeing; everything else estar does = essere
lessons.ai: Give me 'estar' sentences in Spanish and make me decide: stare (progressive or wellbeing) or essere (everything else).

lessons.title: Parlerò

blocks.title: Why this
blocks.text: Same idea as Spanish hablaré: infinitive + endings. One twist: -are verbs change their a to e.

Drop the final -e, and -are becomes -er: parlare → parler-. Then -ò, -ai, -à, -emo, -ete, -anno.
parlerò, parlerai, parlerà, parleremo, parlerete, parleranno.
-ere and -ire just drop the e: scriverò, dormirò. Spell-saver: -care/-gare add an h to stay hard: cercherò, pagherò.
Italians also use the future to guess: sarà vero = será verdad (probably true). Your Spanish does that too.

unlocks: Futuro: stem (-are→-er) + ò, ai, à, emo, ete, anno
lessons.ai: Ask me about my plans for next week and next year using the future. Check that -are verbs switch to -er.

lessons.title: Andrò, sarò, vorrò

blocks.title: Why this
blocks.text: The verbs you use most get shortened stems, like Spanish tendré, podré, querré. Same endings, shorter stem.
Squash: the vowel before -r drops out. andare → andrò, avere → avrò, potere → potrò, dovere → dovrò, sapere → saprò, vedere → vedrò.

Super squash: the stem collapses into a double rr. volere → vorrò, venire → verrò, bere → berrò, tenere → terrò, rimanere → rimarrò.

And the short ones: essere → sarò, fare → farò, dare → darò, stare → starò.

unlocks: Irregular future stems: andr-, avr-, potr-, dovr-, sapr-, vedr-; vorr-, verr-, berr-, terr-; sar-, far-, dar-, star-
lessons.ai: Ask about future plans using the irregular verbs: going, having, being, doing, wanting, coming, being able to.

lessons.title: Parlerei

blocks.title: Why this
blocks.text: The conditional is how you're polite (vorrei, potrebbe) and how you dream (vivrei in Italia). Same stem as the future, new endings. Spanish -ía → Italian -ei.

Future stem + -ei, -esti, -ebbe, -emmo, -este, -ebbero.
parlerei, parleresti, parlerebbe, parleremmo, parlereste, parlerebbero.

Leak: never parlería. And -emmo has a double m (future -emo has one).
The politeness kit: vorrei (quisiera), potrei? (¿podría?), potrebbe…? (¿podría usted…?), dovresti (deberías), mi piacerebbe (me gustaría).

unlocks: Condizionale: future stem + ei, esti, ebbe, emmo, este, ebbero
polite: vorrei, potrei, potrebbe, dovresti, mi piacerebbe
lessons.ai: Role-play ordering, asking favors and giving advice. Then ask what I would do with a free year.

lessons.title: Andrei, sarei, verrei
lessons.decision: the conditional borrows the future's squashed stems

blocks.title: Why this
blocks.text: Zero new stems. Whatever the future did in lesson 28, the conditional does too. You already did the hard part.
Ojo: Italian says venire con te where Spanish often says ir contigo. Moving toward the person you're talking to = venire.

unlocks: Irregular conditional = irregular future stems + -ei endings
lessons.ai: Ask me hypothetical and polite questions that need irregular conditionals.

lessons.title: Parla! Non parlare!

blocks.title: Why this
blocks.text: Commands, for directions, recipes, and telling your friends what to do. Most of it transfers. One rule flips.
tu command for -are verbs = the he/she form, same as Spanish: parla! (¡habla!), mangia!. For -ere/-ire it's the tu form: scrivi!, dormi!, senti!.
The flip: negative tu = non + infinitive. Spanish switches to the subjunctive (no hables). Italian just says non parlare!. Easier, but you'll want to say non parli. Don't.
Pronouns glue on, like Spanish: dimmi! (dime), fammi vedere (déjame ver). Short commands double the consonant: di' + mi = dimmi, fa' + lo = fallo.
Irregular tu commands worth knowing: va' (ve), vieni (ven), fa' (haz), di' (di), sta', abbi pazienza (ten paciencia), sii (sé).

lessons.ai: Have me give directions and advice to a friend with tu commands, including negative ones. Catch 'non parli' for negative tu.

lessons.title: Che tu parli
lessons.decision: the subjunctive flips vowels like Spanish, but more often

blocks.title: Why this
blocks.text: Great news: the Italian subjunctive flips vowels like Spanish (hable → parli). Bad news: Italians use it more. After penso che and credo che (I think that), Italian wants the subjunctive, where Spanish uses the indicative (creo que es).

-are → -i: che io parli, tu parli, lui parli, noi parliamo, voi parliate, loro parlino.
-ere/-ire → -a: scriva, dorma, scriviamo, scriviate, scrivano.

The three singulars are the same, so Italians often add the pronoun: che tu parli.
Here's the leak in reverse: creo que tiene razón → credo che abbia ragione. Spanish indicative, Italian subjunctive. Same for penso che, mi sembra che, non so se.

unlocks: triggers: voglio che, spero che, è importante che, AND penso/credo che (unlike Spanish)
lessons.ai: Give me sentences starting with 'I think that', 'I want that', 'I hope that', and make me use the subjunctive. Flag if I use the indicative after penso che.

lessons.title: Sia, abbia, vada
lessons.decision: essere, avere and the common irregulars

blocks.title: Why this
blocks.text: The verbs you need most have their own subjunctive. Most come from the io present form, like Spanish: hago → haga, faccio → faccia.

essere: sia, sia, sia, siamo, siate, siano (sea).
avere: abbia, abbia, abbia, abbiamo, abbiate, abbiano (tenga / haya).
From the io form: faccio → faccia, vado → vada, vengo → venga, posso → possa, voglio → voglia, devo → debba, dico → dica. And sapere → sappia, stare → stia, dare → dia.

blocks.en: I don't think he can come

blocks.text: Bonus: the formal command is just the subjunctive: mi dica (dígame), venga! (¡venga!), exactly like Spanish usted commands.

unlocks: Irregular congiuntivo: sia, abbia, faccia, vada, venga, possa, voglia, debba, dica, sappia, stia, dia
lessons.ai: Make me react to news with 'I hope that', 'I doubt that', 'it's better that' using irregular subjunctives.

lessons.title: Che parlassi

blocks.title: Why this
blocks.text: The past subjunctive, for wishes about the past and reported wants: quería que hablaras → volevo che parlassi. Spanish speakers have this instinct already.

Drop -re, add -ssi, -ssi, -sse, -ssimo, -ste, -ssero: parlassi, vendessi, dormissi.

Spanish -ara / -iera ↔ Italian -assi / -essi / -issi.
Irregulars: essere → fossi, fossi, fosse, fossimo, foste, fossero (fuera). fare → facessi, dire → dicessi, dare → dessi, stare → stessi.
Magari! = ¡ojalá! (for wishes). Italians say it constantly, also as 'maybe'.

unlocks: essere: fossi…; fare: facessi; dire: dicessi
lessons.ai: Ask what people wanted, hoped and thought in the past so I need the imperfect subjunctive. Throw in 'magari' wishes.

lessons.title: Se potessi, andrei

blocks.title: Why this
blocks.text: The hypothetical: if X were true, I would Y. Spanish and Italian match one-to-one, so this is a reward lesson that strings together the last few.
se + imperfect subjunctive, then conditional. Si tuviera tiempo, viajaría → se avessi tempo, viaggerei. Leak: si is se.

blocks.en: si fuera rico, viviría en Italia
blocks.es: se fossi ricco, vivrei in Italia

blocks.en: if you came, I'd be happy (tú)

blocks.text: And the real-world one, with present + future, is like Spanish too: se piove, resto a casa (si llueve, me quedo en casa).

blocks.en: if it rains, I'll stay home

unlocks: Periodo ipotetico: se + congiuntivo imperfetto, condizionale
lessons.ai: Ask me lots of 'what would you do if…' questions and make me answer in full hypotheticals.

lessons.title: Parlai
lessons.decision: the passato remoto: recognize it, don't stress it

blocks.title: Why this
blocks.text: This is the one-word past your Spanish wanted back in lesson 21. It exists: parlai = hablé. But in most of Italy people barely say it. It's for books, history, and the south. Learn to recognize it.
parlai, parlasti, parlò, parlammo, parlaste, parlarono. Compare hablé, hablaste, habló, hablamos, hablasteis, hablaron. Family resemblance, right?
You'll mostly meet the 'he/she' and 'they' forms in stories: fu (fue), ebbe (tuvo), disse (dijo), fece (hizo), venne (vino), nacque (nació).
In speech, though: ieri sono andato, not ieri andai, unless you're in Sicily or Naples. Then everyone says it and you'll fit right in.

unlocks: common irregulars: fu, ebbe, disse, fece, venne, nacque
lessons.ai: Tell me a short story in the passato remoto, then ask me to retell it in the passato prossimo.

lessons.title: Si parla italiano

blocks.title: Why this
blocks.text: Se habla español, ¿cómo se dice? Italian does the exact same with si. Final lesson, and it's a gimme, plus a phrase you'll use every day.
si + he/she form: si parla italiano. Plural thing → plural verb: si vendono case (se venden casas).

blocks.en: how do you get to the station?

blocks.text: Come si dice…? and Come si scrive? (how do you spell it) are your survival tools for real conversation. Use them every time you're stuck, in Italian, and you never have to drop to English.
Que ya. That's the whole MTC grammar sequence. From here the work is listening and talking: log real Italian on the Immersion card, and use the robot button to practice. Forza!

unlocks: come si dice? / come si scrive?
lessons.ai: Ask me 'how do you say / how does one do' questions about life in Italy, so I use the si construction. Then free conversation using everything.
